prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the claims-triage agent (home and motor claims assessment within delegated authority) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: a leak from the flat upstairs. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 1)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When the leak is from a flat upstairs, I should separate the source of the water from the extent of the damage below, because stopping the leak whether the upstairs resident owns or rents the flat, as that often changes who is responsible for access, repairs and any possible recovery route."},{"type":"observation","content":"When water has active water can rapidly increase the loss."},{"type":"fact","content":"When multiple flats are affected, I should note the pattern of damage floor by floor, because a single leak can create several related claims or one shared event depending on how the building is arranged."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the water appears to have travelled along pipes, joists or service voids, I should be cautious about underestimating the affected area, as the worst damage is sometimes away from the drip point."},{"type":"preference","content":"When there is any electrical fitting, light, or socket near the water path, I prefer to flag potential safety risk immediately, because safe re-occupation matters more than a quick repair estimate."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the upstairs flat is occupied but the resident is unavailable, I should still record what can be seen externally and what access is needed, because delay in gaining entry is often the main reason a small leak becomes a larger one."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the damage is mainly staining rather than wetness, I should avoid assuming the claim is minor, because old water can hide ongoing seepage or
